title: City Council Infrastructure and Facilities Meeting
overview: The Wausau City Council Infrastructure and Facilities Committee met and approved several items related to the South 11th Avenue reconstruction project affecting Kolbe and Kolbe Millwork, including handicap parking additions and multiple driveway variances. The committee also discussed the formation of a Boulevard Beautification Special Committee, initiated a conversation about selling or offloading city-owned vacant parcels, and held an extended discussion on fall leaf collection operations, costs, and future contract considerations. No major items were rejected; most business passed unanimously with minimal debate.

discussions.item: Handicap Parking on North Second Street, McCloud Street, and Grant Street
discussions.body: Staff explained the request came from Church of the Resurrection to add two more handicap stalls, and that two stalls added during the Second Street reconstruction had not been codified in the ordinance. The committee moved to approve the item to both add new stalls and clean up the ordinance. The motion passed unanimously with no discussion.

discussions.item: Preliminary Resolution for Special Assessment for 2027 Street Construction Projects
discussions.body: Staff described the item as self-explanatory, noting approval would allow the city to set public hearings on special assessments, typically in December, in order to begin bidding projects. The motion was seconded by Wisowsky and passed unanimously with no discussion.

discussions.item: Kolbe and Kolbe Millwork Driveway and Approach Variances (Items 4C–4F)
discussions.body: Staff explained that the South 11th Avenue reconstruction project required coordinating with Kolbe and Kolbe Millwork, whose campus straddles the road, over multiple meetings. The committee approved lay-down curb instead of full-head curb to preserve perpendicular parking at 1323 South 11th Avenue, waived the concrete approach requirement (staff noted asphalt costs roughly one-quarter the price of concrete at approximately $2 versus $8.50 per square foot), and approved two additional oversized driveways at 1330 and 1320 South 11th Avenue. A question about stormwater impact of the larger driveway was answered by staff, who called it minimal. All four items passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Recommendation to Extend Sidewalk on South 11th Avenue from Chellis Street to Fleith Street
discussions.body: Staff proposed adding sidewalk on the west side of 11th Avenue primarily to provide safe passage for Kolbe workers crossing to the manufacturing facility, with future connectivity potential toward 3M Park. Questions were raised about cost (staff said it would be a 50/50 cost share but did not have figures available) and whether bike lanes were planned (confirmed they were not). The motion was initially overlooked before being made and seconded by Alderman Martin; the item passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Boulevard Beautification Special Committee Formation
discussions.body: Kilian announced the formation of a special committee (not a subcommittee, as it includes public members) authorized by the October 27 council resolution. Appointed members include Alder Wiskowski as chair, city engineer Alan Wislowski PE, and citizen members Tim Hau, Dave Nutting, and Trevor Frank. All appointments are pending city council approval at the next meeting. Discussion briefly touched on a possible pre-Christmas organizational meeting, though some members noted travel conflicts in December.

discussions.item: City-Owned Vacant Parcels
discussions.body: Alder Wiskowski raised the topic, expressing interest in identifying city-owned vacant parcels with no development plans in order to offload them — particularly small slivers — back onto the tax rolls, potentially by selling to adjacent property owners. Other members raised questions about contamination (noting 1300 Cleveland is known to be contaminated), how the city acquired the parcels, and whether some listed as 'vacant' are actually serving purposes such as water retention. The committee agreed to bring the item back at the next meeting with a refined, narrowed list removing parcels already slated for development or serving active purposes, and directed staff to consult with Eric and Randy on contamination status.

discussions.item: Fall Leaf Collection Operations and Future Contracts
discussions.body: Alder Slansky raised constituent confusion about multiple leaf pickup rounds; Public Works staff member Dustin appeared and explained the city guarantees one full pass through the city with a baler, with follow-up vac trucks and sweepers that residents misinterpret as additional scheduled collections. Dustin noted complaints were actually down this year after consolidating to a single-phase map. The committee learned that all relevant contracts — tractor/baler, bale hauling, and yard waste — are expiring, and the current farmer-partner does not want to renew; the city may need to lease-to-own a baler. Alder Wiskowski raised the possibility of reducing or modifying leaf collection given the roughly $400,000–$500,000 annual cost, while Alder Martin cautioned that leaf collection helps reduce phosphorus and total dissolved solids discharging into the Wisconsin River under the TMDL requirements. Staff also explained that to earn DNR leaf credits, the city would need three to four collection rounds per neighborhood and an ordinance prohibiting leaves in the roadway — requirements currently unmet. The committee agreed to bring leaf collection back as a full agenda item in January, including contract options, communication improvements, service level expectations, and sustainability considerations.

title: Board Executive Committee Meeting Pt.2
overview: The Marathon County Board Executive Committee held the second part of its meeting, covering an agenda packet timeline update from administration and a discussion about improving the timeliness of packet materials for committee chairs. No major votes were taken; the meeting concluded with a motion to adjourn and a note that an additional county board meeting is scheduled for November 17th at 6:00 p.m.

discussions.item: Agenda Packet Timeline Update
discussions.body: Administration staff, led by what appears to be the county administrator and County Clerk Kim, presented an update on the agenda and packet preparation process, describing it as functioning like an agenda management system without dedicated software. The administrator emphasized that a note in the document stating packets are 'final and will not be amended without administration approval' was intended as a gate on staff — not on committee chairs — clarifying that chairs retain full authority over their agendas. Supervisor Rosemarie praised the current system, saying it was a marked improvement over past practices at other entities she had experienced.

discussions.item: Committee Chair Roles and Packet Timeliness
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson raised concerns about receiving packet materials too late — only by 8:00 a.m. on Friday mornings — saying that as a standing committee chair, he sometimes reviews memos and concludes items are 'not ready for prime time' but lacks time to act on that before the meeting. He asserted that policy-setting committee chairs, not administration, should be primary in setting agendas. The administrator acknowledged the feedback and noted that historically packet items were distributed in paper with no advance chair review, and that accommodating earlier chair review of packets would require reworking the current timeline and potentially the board rules.

discussions.item: Potential Revision of Packet Timeline and Board Rules
discussions.body: Board Chair Gibbs asked whether the timeline needed to be backed up by a couple of days to accommodate Supervisor Robinson's concerns. The administrator indicated that if chairs want earlier access to packet items, the entire process would need to be redesigned, as that level of chair oversight has not previously been built into the system. It was noted that this may also require revisions to board rules. No action was taken; the item was informational only, and Supervisor Robinson was jokingly suggested as a task force chair on the topic.

title: Board Executive Committee Meeting Pt.1
overview: The Marathon County Board Executive Committee held a wide-ranging meeting covering the Bugtussle bond default crisis, the Hub City Wind Farm joint development agreement, a county road funding policy, and strategic plan updates. The committee voted unanimously to enter closed session to discuss strategy related to Bugtussle's failure to make payments on a $25 million conduit bond, leaving the county on the hook for a $347,409 shortfall, and also agreed to call a special full board meeting for the following Tuesday at 6 p.m. to address both the Alliant/Hub City Wind JDA response and the Bugtussle situation.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Two speakers addressed the committee. Joe Bergen of the Town of Day criticized the Alliant/Hub City Wind Farm proposed Joint Development Agreement (JDA) as vague and one-sided, noting provisions such as 90-day complaint response windows and unspecified haul routes, and urged the county to disregard the JDA and draft its own protective agreement. Ed Ruschinski, town chairman of Bergen, spoke about Moon Road, which accesses Big Oplain Park, arguing that the town maintains the road without property tax revenue from the park and requesting county funding assistance; he also suggested the county consider a user fee for horse trailer use on trails.

discussions.body: Supervisor Maras moved approval and Supervisor Rosenberg seconded. No discussion was held and the minutes were approved unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Strategic Plan Development Update and Next Steps
discussions.body: Vice Chair Boots reported that the 20 draft strategic objectives had been sent to the public and returned, with compilation planned for November and an informational packet expected for the December executive meeting. Staff discussed potentially adding data points for every strategy, not just each objective, which may push final adoption to January or February 2027. Supervisor Deb [last name inaudible] raised a concern that strategic plan language promoting agricultural land preservation conflicted with wind and solar development; Boots and staff noted that even if included, state statutes governing projects over 100 megawatts would still control. Approximately 150 public responses were received.

discussions.item: Comprehensive Revision to Ordinances to Reference Fee Schedule
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard briefly described the proposal to remove specific fee dollar amounts from ordinances and reference the newly adopted fee schedule instead. Supervisor Robinson raised concerns that some items — including Children with Disabilities Educational Board compensation, Civil Service Commission pay, vehicle registration fees, and statutorily set delinquent property tax percentages — were not appropriate for this process. Administration agreed to provide a redlined version and the committee voted unanimously to postpone action to the December executive committee meeting.

discussions.item: County Policy Regarding Funding of Town Roadways Providing Access to County Facilities (Moon Road and Duncan Road)
discussions.body: Deputy Administrator Homan and Director Pauley presented updates to a 2015 resolution governing county assistance to towns for roads accessing county parks and forest units, including two newly proposed additions: a section of Moon Road (Town of Bergen to Big Oplain Park) and Leather Camp Drive (Town of Bavent). Extensive debate followed on where to draw policy lines, particularly regarding highway facilities like the Kronenwetter salt shed and whether the resolution should expand beyond parks and forests. Supervisor Greiner supported gathering traffic count data specifically for Moon Road given its unique situation as the only county park with this access issue. Supervisor Boots, Robinson, and Ritter expressed caution about expanding scope without more research. The committee voted unanimously to postpone to no later than the January executive committee meeting, with administration directed to gather maps, traffic count methodology, historical cost data since 2015, information on peer county practices, any legal requirements for such a policy, existing township road agreements, and tonnage impacts from forestry operations.

discussions.item: Item 6D: Alliant/Hub City Wind JDA and Special Board Meeting
discussions.body: Chair Gibbs explained that Marathon County Resolution 5526 required the Alliant/Hub City Wind proposed JDA to be brought before the full board. He proposed calling a special board meeting the following Tuesday at 6 p.m. to allow all 38 board members to weigh in on a response — whether further negotiation, revision, or termination of discussions. The committee reached consensus on Tuesday evening and Gibbs said he would notify all board members to reserve that date.

discussions.item: Bugtussle Relationship Update and Discussion of Special Board Meeting
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard recapped the Bugtussle bond default: Bugtussle failed to deposit required funds into the debt service fund by October 15, received default notices on October 26-27, and the trustee made a November 2 payment from reserves. Bugtussle has failed to replenish the fund, leaving a shortfall of $347,409.01 that the county must pay under its guarantee by April 8, 2027. The county's annual obligation on the $25 million conduit issuance runs approximately $1,504,443 per year through 2051. The committee voted unanimously by roll call to enter closed session under Wisconsin Statutes 19.85(1)(e) and 19.85(1)(g) to discuss asset recovery strategy and potential litigation without revealing the county's hand to Bugtussle.

publicComment: Two speakers offered public comment. Joe Bergen, Town of Day, criticized the Hub City Wind Farm proposed JDA as vague, one-sided, and inadequate — citing a 90-day complaint response window, unspecified haul routes, no decommissioning bonding, and lump-sum road repair provisions — and urged the county to reject it and draft its own protective agreement. Ed Ruschinski, town chairman of Bergen, requested county funding assistance for Moon Road, which accesses Big Oplain Park, arguing the town receives no property tax from the park's roughly 900 acres in Bergen despite heavy road traffic, and suggested the county consider a horse trailer user fee for park trails.

committee: City of Wausau Joint Finance and Human Resources Committee
overview: The Wausau Joint Finance and Human Resources Committee met on November 10, 2026, addressing a range of items including a 3% salary scale increase for general employees, a contentious sole-source purchase of Zoll cardiac monitors and ventilators for the fire department, lead service line funding amendments, and year-end budget modifications. The most significant debate centered on the fire department equipment purchase totaling $214,521, with disagreement over how future payments would be funded before the item ultimately passed 4-1.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Courtney Olsen of Highland Park Boulevard spoke on item 2G, the 2026 year-end budget modifications. She expressed support for the committee's prior 5-0 vote to remove a $50,000 Flock Safety camera payment from the 2027 budget and move it to motor pool expenses. She urged the committee to request a written opinion from the city attorney confirming that the next Flock invoice belongs to the 2027 budget and that the city can exit the contract under Section 11.16 without penalty, and asked that written notice be sent to Flock by November 15 to terminate the contract before a December invoice is generated.

discussions.item: Revised Salary Structure for General Employees (Joint HR/Finance)
discussions.body: Human Resources staff presented a proposed 3% cost-of-living increase to the wage scale for non-represented general employees and seasonals, citing a 4.2% CPI-U increase and a 3.6% Social Security COLA. The presenter noted this is consistent with negotiated increases for transit (3.5% in 2026, 3% in 2027) and below the 4% increases for police and fire in 2027. Both the HR and Finance committees voted to approve without notable opposition; Alder Larson moved for HR and Alder Killion seconded; a separate motion carried for Finance.

discussions.item: Sole Source Request — Zoll Monitors and Ventilators for Fire Department
discussions.body: EMS Division Chief Matt O'Mullen presented a sole-source request totaling $214,521 for new cardiac monitors (reaching end of 8-year service life) and ventilators (over 15 years old with no available maintenance). He argued that purchasing both together before an April 2027 price increase saved approximately $40,000 through grouped pricing, avoided warranty costs, and trade-in value, with the first year's payment (~$40,000) covered by FAP (Fire Ambulance Program) funds. Alder Tierney questioned why the item was not in the 2027 budget and expressed reluctance to support it without a commitment to use FAP dollars in future years. Alder Hanke moved an amendment requiring 15% of subsequent four annual payments to come from FAP, but it was withdrawn after Alder Neal argued the payment structure was separate from the sole-source approval. A further amendment to strike payment language from the motion passed 4-1 (Tierney opposed), and the amended sole-source request then passed 4-1 with Tierney opposed. The committee acknowledged a financing agreement with Zoll would need to return to committee and council.

discussions.item: 2027 Operating Plan for Business Improvement District No. 1
discussions.body: The committee approved the 2027 operating plan for BID No. 1, the downtown River District, with no notable discussion. Alder Watson moved, Alder Neal seconded, and it passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 2027 Beat Patrol Grant for Wausau Police Department
discussions.body: The committee approved the recurring Beat Patrol Grant for the police department. Alder Watson asked where the $40,000 city match would come from and was told it is already included in the 2027 budget. Watson then moved to approve; Alder Neal seconded; passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Budget Amendment for 2027 Lead Service Line Safe Drinking Water Award
discussions.body: Finance Director Mary Ann presented last-minute changes to the lead service line funding: anticipated principal forgiveness dropped from $7.9 million to just under $5 million, and the utility loan rate increased from 0.25% to 2.585% due to program competitiveness statewide, increasing net city borrowing by approximately $1.5 million on the homeowner side and $1.95 million on the utility side. Alder Neal moved to approve and Alder Watson seconded, but Watson withdrew her second after expressing concern that the committee had insufficient time to analyze the changes. Without a second, the motion died. overview: The Wausau City Council held its November 10, 2026 regular meeting, passing the 2027 City of Wausau budget 7-4 after lengthy debate over the budget process, borrowing levels, and spending priorities. The council also heard a mayoral presentation on a potential city administrator position, approved several proclamations, and unanimously passed numerous other resolutions including designation of Yawkey Park as a local historic landmark.

discussions.item: City Administrator Presentation
discussions.body: Mayor Diny presented an update on the city administrator proposal, noting a public survey had received 296 responses with a week remaining, and that roughly 70% of Wisconsin cities have some form of professional city management. Alder Tierney questioned whether the $150,000 budget figure was well-supported, noting uncertainty about actual annual cost including benefits, which the mayor estimated at $150,000–$200,000 per year. Alder Henecke expressed skepticism that adding an administrator position would tangibly address residents' systemic concerns, while Alder Neal said he wanted comparative salary data before proceeding. Alder Wiskowski asked about multiple models, including a deputy mayor or chief of staff option. The mayor said the city attorney's office is ready to draft ordinance language and proposed a committee of the whole as the next step, but no vote was taken on the proposal.

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes from October 27th Regular Council Meeting
discussions.body: Alder Lukens requested a correction to the minutes clarifying that his action during a vote on the Flock data resolution was a question, not an objection. The council voted to amend the minutes to reflect this clarification, then approved the minutes as amended, passing 11-0.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Four speakers addressed the council. Courtney Olsen, executive director of a domestic violence agency, urged the council to send written termination notice to Flock by November 15th and to exclude Flock payments from the 2027 and 2028 budgets, noting cameras had already been covered by Public Works. Amelia Wajchowski read a statement from Yawkey heirs supporting the historic landmark designation of Yawkey Park. Christine Martins also urged support for the Yawkey Park landmarking. Danielle Fischer echoed support for terminating the Flock contract and also endorsed the city audit.

discussions.item: 2027 City of Wausau Budget — Amendment to Use Reserves for Debt Offset
discussions.body: Alder Henecke moved to amend the 2027 budget to draw from the city's approximately $16 million in reserves to offset new borrowing so that net new debt would be zero — meaning the city would borrow no more than the roughly $18 million it was paying down, rather than the planned $22 million. Finance Director Mary Ann Groat cautioned that Wausau's unassigned fund balance as a percent of general fund expenses is already on the lower end compared to peer cities, and recommended against the drawdown at this time. Alder Watson, Alder Martens, and Alder Slansky also spoke against the amendment, citing bond rating concerns and existing reserve policy that limits use to unanticipated, non-recurring needs. The amendment failed 2-9.

discussions.item: 2027 City of Wausau Budget — Main Motion
discussions.body: The main budget vote followed extended debate. Alder Wiskowski expressed frustration with the lack of full-council deliberation outside the finance committee, and asked Finance Director Groat to confirm the projected impact: a $71.52 increase for a $200,000 home, driven approximately 60% by the voter-approved addition of 12 firefighter-paramedics. Alder Trueblood and Alder Lukens expressed reservations and indicated they would have preferred more time and public input. Alder Tierney challenged budget opponents to identify specific cuts. Finance Committee Chair Martens summarized key amendments already baked in: $150,000 redirected from city administrator to audit, $50,000 for Flock eliminated, $45,000 for alley paving eliminated, $20,000 for trail planning eliminated, $150,000 for downtown traffic design engineering removed, and $2.5 million in lead service line replacements moved to TID 8. The budget passed 7-4.

discussions.item: Yawkey Park Historic Landmark Designation (Consent Agenda)
discussions.body: The designation of Yawkey Park as a local historic landmark was included on the consent agenda and passed unanimously 11-0. Mayor Diny noted it had previously passed unanimously through the Plan Commission and Historic Preservation Committee. A written statement from Yawkey heirs was read into the record supporting the designation.

discussions.item: Beat Patrol Grant — Wausau Police Department
discussions.body: Police Chief addressed questions from Alder Henecke and others about the $121,434 Wisconsin DOJ Beat Patrol Grant, noting it effectively funds approximately two officers and that Wausau qualifies as one of the ten Wisconsin communities with the highest crime levels relative to population. The chief acknowledged that if the grant were lost, a difficult conversation with the council about staffing and funding would follow. Alder Henecke expressed concern that federal police reform efforts could jeopardize future grant funding. The resolution passed unanimously 11-0.

publicComment: Four speakers offered public comment. Courtney Olsen (Highland Park Boulevard), executive director of a domestic violence agency, urged the council to send written contract termination notice to Flock Safety by November 15th and to exclude all remaining Flock payments from the budget, citing a contract clause allowing exit without penalty via non-appropriation. Amelia Wajchowski, assistant director of the Leigh Yawkey Woodson Art Museum, read a statement from Yawkey heirs — Alice Woodson Smith, A. Woodson Hagge, Abigail Spire, Leigh Tuckey, and Nancy Leigh Fischer — expressing full support for the Yawkey Park historic landmark designation. Christine Martins (1228 Arthur Street) also urged support for the Yawkey Park landmarking. Danielle Fischer (1212 Highland Park Boulevard) supported terminating the Flock contract and endorsed the city audit. One additional person spoke during the budget public hearing, expressing support for the audit over the city administrator position and objecting to the administrator proposal moving forward without a referendum.

title: (Budget) Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Board of Supervisors held its annual budget meeting on November 10, 2026, taking up the 2027 budget and property tax levy along with several amendments. Key debates centered on a proposed $1.75 million reduction to the tax levy (defeated), and whether to continue funding Flock license plate reader cameras in the sheriff's department budget (ultimately moved to contingency pending policy review). The meeting drew a near-capacity crowd and reflected significant tension between fiscal conservatives seeking levy reductions and those defending the county's highway shop funding strategy.

discussions.item: C13C — Sale of Tax Deeded Property for $1 (Resolution 77-26)
discussions.body: Supervisor Straub objected to selling the property for $1, arguing it was worth $25,000–$45,000 and that the county could have demolished the mold-infested structure itself cheaply. Supervisor Robinson countered that a certified appraiser valued the property at zero due to severe mold contamination, that the city would demolish it and return it to housing stock, and that accepting the transfer relieved the county of remediation liability. The motion to approve the $1 sale passed but was not unanimous.

discussions.item: D14A — ATV/UTV Ordinance on Highway 34 (Ordinance 53-26)
discussions.body: Supervisor Hoppa raised safety concerns about lighting on the bridge where ATVs and UTVs would share the road. The Highway Commissioner confirmed no additional county lighting was planned since it is a state road, and noted ATVs are required to have headlights and taillights when operating on roads. Supervisor Neiseth expressed concern about the 55 mph speed limit on the corridor but was told speed limits are state-controlled. Supervisor Mask encouraged support, citing constituents' safety concerns. The ordinance passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget — Amendment 5: $1.75 Million Tax Levy Reduction
discussions.body: Supervisor Sandelski moved to reduce the proposed tax levy increase by $1.75 million, funded by drawing from the highway fund rather than debt levy, arguing the county's 8% levy increase was 'egregious' and that highway fund reserves were healthy. County Administrator Leonard and Supervisor Robinson gave extensive rebuttals, explaining that the highway fund balance is nearly fully committed to the $55 million highway shop project and that the interfund loan strategy was the least costly approach. Supervisors Dickinson, Straub, and Cavelli spoke in favor of the amendment, while Vice Chair Boes and Robinson urged rejection given the Bug Tussle broadband financial liability also looming. Debate was closed by a two-thirds vote after Supervisor Krebs called the question. The amendment was defeated.

discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson moved to remove $6,300 for Flock license plate reader cameras from the Sheriff's Department hardware/software budget and place it in the HR Finance Committee contingency fund, pending policy discussions between Sheriff Billick and privacy advocate Mr. Gallo on data retention, access, and audit requirements. Supervisor Neiseth moved an amendment to instead eliminate the $6,300 entirely and reduce the tax levy, citing Fourth Amendment concerns and constituent opposition. That amendment to the amendment failed. Robinson's original amendment — moving funds to contingency — then passed, though not unanimously, with the understanding that policy discussions would occur at Public Safety and HR Finance committees before any funds are released.

publicComment: No formal public comment period was held at this meeting, though Supervisor Trapp read extensively from a Wausau Pilot and Review investigative article by Shereen Siewert (published November 3–4, 2026) reporting that 1,410 law enforcement agencies across 40 states can search Marathon County's Flock camera data, contradicting Sheriff Billick's earlier public statements. References were also made to testimony from a citizen named Mr. Gallo at the prior week's public hearing regarding privacy concerns over Flock cameras.

overview: The Marathon County Public Safety Committee held its November 2026 meeting focused heavily on the Sheriff's Office's Flock automatic license plate reader (ALPR) program, with significant public input and committee debate over data privacy, oversight, and whether to defund the cameras. The committee also received presentations on the Sheriff's Office drone program and a 2027 budget overview. No formal votes were taken at the committee level, though a budget amendment moving $6,300 in Flock funding to a contingency fund was noted as pending a full County Board vote that evening.

discussions.body: One supervisor objected to approving the minutes, alleging that his request to place Flock cameras on the October agenda was deflected off-camera by Administrator Lance Leonard, and that this was not captured in the record. The clerk explained that minutes only capture motions and actions, with video timestamps serving as the official record. The chair noted that Lance Leonard helps set agendas and that is why members are referred to him. The objecting supervisor refused to approve the minutes; the motion carried over his objection with the majority voting aye, though no specific tally was stated.

discussions.item: 2027 Annual Budget Overview - Flock ALPR Funding
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson (referred to by others) explained that the Human Resources Finance and Property Committee had reviewed an amendment to move $6,300 budgeted for Flock cameras into a contingency fund, contingent on resolving concerns about access, oversight, and data retention. County Administrator Lance Leonard and Corporation Counsel Brian [inaudible] clarified that the county board cannot directly control sheriff's operational contracts due to the sheriff's status as a constitutional officer, creating a legal gray area. Committee members questioned whether pulling funding would actually force cameras down and whether future contracts would require board approval; both questions were left largely unresolved pending further legal analysis.

discussions.item: Sheriff's Office Drone Program
discussions.body: Sheriff Chad Bileb presented the drone program, noting the office operates three types of drones used for crash investigations, search and rescue, building clearing, and community events. The team includes approximately seven members, with three or four Part 107 FAA-certified pilots. Captain Seibert was present to answer technical questions. Committee members asked about recreational drone pilots potentially assisting or interfering with law enforcement operations; the sheriff indicated legal liability and HR concerns would preclude using volunteer pilots, and that recreational operators are not required to submit footage unless legally compelled.

discussions.item: Flock ALPR Contract Update and Committee Discussion
discussions.body: Sheriff Bileb addressed the committee's previously submitted questions: the office contracts for eight Falcon ALPR cameras funded by Wisconsin DOJ grants, plus two operated for the Village of Rib Mountain; cameras are located on I-39 and State Highway 29; early termination costs are $500 per camera. The sheriff acknowledged that up to 1,580 agencies have sharing access and that, following feedback from Felix Gallo, Captain Stefanik is auditing and significantly reducing that list. The sheriff maintained that Marathon County does not subscribe to Flock's traffic analytics product and that raw data is deleted after 30 days, but acknowledged disagreement with Gallo on what the contract's perpetual license covers. Multiple supervisors and non-committee county board members spoke against the program, citing mass surveillance concerns, Fourth Amendment issues, and lack of independent oversight, while supervisors Hoppa and one other expressed support or ambivalence, noting real public safety benefits. Sheriff Bileb stated he would not voluntarily remove the cameras, and indicated he expects state legislation on ALPR to emerge in the upcoming session.

publicComment: Felix Gallo of Highland Park in Wausau spoke during public comment, raising detailed concerns about the Flock ALPR contract's data retention terms. He argued that the contract's perpetual data license (sections 4, 5, and 6.6) survives termination and is not limited to 30 days, contradicting the sheriff's office memo. He warned that images can be downloaded by thousands of external agencies during the first 30 days and retained indefinitely, and that so-called 'de-identified' aggregate data can be used by Flock for future products. He also flagged that the office was not auditing searches by the 1,500-plus external agencies with access. Additionally, Supervisor David Nyceath of District 21 (not a committee member) spoke at length during the Flock discussion, urging the committee to defund the cameras, citing Fourth Amendment concerns, risk of data breaches, mission creep, and the precedent set by Wausau's 9-1 vote to cover its cameras. Supervisor Joel [inaudible] read aloud a citizen group statement summarizing a Wausau Pilot and Review investigative report alleging discrepancies between what the sheriff told supervisors and what the office's own records and policies show.

title: Village Board Meeting
overview: The Village of Kronenwetter Board held its November 9, 2026 meeting primarily to adopt the 2027 operating budget, including all three budget resolutions covering the general fund, all other funds, and the capital improvements program. The board also formally appointed Connie Nowak as village clerk and renewed its legal services agreement with Wolfram, Gamoke and Hutchinson. All items passed unanimously 7-0, with Finance Director John presenting a detailed budget overview highlighting a proposed assessed tax rate of $4.25, a 6.79% tax levy increase, and no water or sewer rate increases for 2027.

discussions.item: Public Hearing - 2027 Operating Budget
discussions.body: One member of the public, identified as Bernie, spoke during the public hearing. He commented on the state levy limit calculations, the disparity between Kronenwetter's high residential tax base (84%) versus commercial-heavy communities like Schofield (39%), questioned the need for a deputy clerk given Friday office closures, and expressed strong opposition to the village's ethics committee, calling it 'totally meaningless.' No other members of the public spoke during the hearing.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Presentation
discussions.body: Finance Director John presented a detailed budget overview. Key highlights included a proposed assessed tax rate of $4.25 (equalized equivalent of $2.71), a total tax levy of approximately $2.9 million representing a 6.79% increase, no water or sewer rate increases, a garbage fee increase of $39.24 largely due to a diesel fuel surcharge, and a 3.5% COLA for non-elected positions. John noted the village's unassigned fund balance has grown from 3.52% in 2023 to approximately 34% for 2025, and previewed that a 2027 revaluation will likely drop the assessed tax rate significantly in 2028. Trustee Coyle thanked staff for presenting a 'competent budget,' implicitly referencing past budget shortfalls in 2023-2024 when debt service was underfunded by approximately $1.2 million over two years.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-013 - Adopt 2027 General Fund Operating Budget
discussions.body: Trustee Lesniak moved and Trustee Stowell seconded adoption of the 2027 general fund operating budget with a total appropriation of $6.5 million and a tax levy increase of 6.79%. The resolution passed unanimously 7-0 on roll call vote with no dissent or notable debate.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-014 - Adopt 2027 Budget for Debt Service, Special Revenue, Capital Projects, and Proprietary Funds
discussions.body: Trustee Stowell moved and Trustee Mishka seconded adoption of the resolution covering all other funds including debt service, special revenue, capital projects, TID districts, and utility funds. The resolution passed unanimously 7-0 on roll call with no discussion.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-015 - Adopt 2027 Capital Improvements Program Budget
discussions.body: Trustee Coyle moved and Trustee Solheim seconded adoption of the 2027 CIP budget totaling approximately $4.3 million, with proposed general obligation borrowing of roughly $1.865 million. John clarified that approving the CIP budget does not authorize immediate borrowing; separate borrowing resolutions must come before the board in 2027. The resolution passed unanimously 7-0.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-016 - Appointment of Connie Nowak as Village Clerk
discussions.body: Trustee Mishka moved and Trustee Mortensen seconded appointing Connie Nowak as village clerk. Finance Director John flagged a potential error in the resolution's first 'whereas' clause, noting the charter ordinance specifies April as the start of the term rather than October; the board agreed to accept an abbreviated appointment now and clean up the language consistent with charter requirements. Multiple trustees praised Nowak, with Joling noting residents had already given her positive feedback. The resolution passed unanimously 7-0.

discussions.item: Legal Services Agreement with Wolfram, Gamoke and Hutchinson
discussions.body: Trustee Mortensen moved and Trustee Solheim seconded approval of the legal services agreement. Brief discussion noted the contract is essentially the same as the existing one and that Village Attorney Wolfram has been well regarded, including by the former police chief. The agreement passed unanimously 7-0.

discussions.item: Future Agenda Items
discussions.body: Village Administrator Jim raised the possibility of moving from two board meetings per month to one meeting per month on the fourth Monday, framing it as a way to streamline committee-to-board workflow and reduce scheduling burdens on trustees. He noted an ordinance change would be required and indicated it would be a discussion item at the next meeting. Discussion also touched on the rationale for Friday afternoon office closures, with staff explaining that uninterrupted time is needed for meeting minutes and audit tasks, and that a deputy clerk hire is planned for late first quarter 2027.

He commented on the state levy limit worksheet and debt service adjustment figures, challenged the accuracy of per-capita tax comparisons between Kronenwetter (317 per capita, 84% residential) and commercial-heavy communities like Schofield (39% residential), questioned the proposed deputy clerk position given the village's Friday afternoon office closure policy, and criticized the village ethics committee as 'totally meaningless' and unworkable. No other members of the public spoke.

title: Public Works Committee
overview: The Village of Weston Public Works Committee held its regular meeting on November 10, 2026, covering a detailed infiltration and inflow (I&I) study presentation for the Rothschild sewer basin, a sewer rate increase recommendation, and approvals of several intergovernmental agreements and design contracts. Key decisions included recommending Option F for 2027 sewer rates, approving a pedestrian crossing design contract at County Trunk X and Sternberg Avenue, approving a storm pond construction agreement, and approving an intergovernmental agreement with the Town of Weston for Ross Avenue reconstruction.

discussions.item: I&I Study Presentation
discussions.body: Sean Dudy of Inpipe Technology presented results of a 44-day infiltration and inflow study covering approximately 26,000 feet of sewer pipe in the Rothschild area south of Highway 29. The study identified two 'red' priority areas — basin 2 and basin 3 — totaling about 3,300 feet, where groundwater infiltration and rain-driven inflow were highest, with one area showing 500-600% flow increases during rain events. Staff noted they had already identified a low manhole in one hot spot and discussed potential slip lining as a remediation tool. Committee members asked about flow volumes (approximately 1.9 to 5 gallons per minute in problem areas) and whether CCTV inspection had been done; staff confirmed historical televising exists but has not yet targeted these specific areas. Staff framed the study as providing data-driven direction to focus limited maintenance dollars rather than treating the entire neighborhood.

discussions.item: VIP (Village Improvement Projects) Update
discussions.body: Public Works Director Michael provided updates on numerous active projects: Weston A special assessments are expected for the board next Monday; Scullfield A has concrete work remaining for spring 2027 with Treweiler as subcontractor; Bladl Avenue final paving is complete; Concord and Bayberry paving began the morning of the meeting; Ross Avenue Metro to Alderson project is targeted for February bid; Fuller Street punch list work was completed. The Ross Avenue and County Road X design contract (item 14) was previewed, with committee members raising concerns about insurance and liability limitation language in the consultant contract. Staff confirmed they would align the contract with the village's standard attorney-reviewed template before board execution.

discussions.item: Street Operations Update
discussions.body: Staff reported completion of storm sewer work at wells 7 and 8 near the golf course, reconstruction of the outfall structure at Kathy Street including a new trash guard to prevent children from entering the pipe, overlay of Heron Street's northbound lane using a combination of contracted RC Pavers equipment and village-hauled asphalt, and replacement of a culvert on Harney Avenue. Fall curbside yard waste and leaf pickup operations were described as requiring at least four DPW staff members daily, with vac trucks averaging 10 loads each at 20 cubic yards per load. A committee member asked staff to quantify the cost savings from using in-house labor alongside contracted paving services; staff agreed to compile those figures for the December meeting, noting two competing bids differed by about $15,000.

discussions.item: 2027 Sanitary Sewer Rate Policy Discussion and Recommendation
discussions.body: Staff presented updated rate options following the previous month's discussion, noting that simply breaking even (Option A) was not considered viable by committee members. Discussion centered on Options G (projected net income ~$160,000) and F (projected net revenue ~$113,000). One member noted that at average usage of 12,000 gallons per year, the difference between G and F is roughly $5 per quarter or $20 per year per household. Committee members cited the need for funds to support slip lining projects, rising Mountain Metro treatment costs (up nearly $800,000 since 2019), and aging infrastructure including 10 miles of asbestos water main. The committee voted to recommend Option F, with staff noting rates could be lowered in future years if significant surplus developed.

discussions.item: Sidewalk Snow Removal Policy
discussions.body: Discussion was prompted by a resident letter from someone abutting Fuller Street who is handicapped and cannot clear their sidewalk. Committee members unanimously agreed that creating an individual exception would be unworkable and set a problematic precedent, with one member stating 'if you don't follow it, you just don't even have one really.' The committee voted to make no substantive change to the snow removal policy but directed staff to update the written policy to reflect current actual practices, including newly added paths not previously listed. One member suggested the village newsletter could solicit volunteer 'sidewalk angels' to assist residents in need; staff agreed to include that in the newsletter.

discussions.item: County Trunk X and Sternberg Avenue Pedestrian Design Contract
discussions.body: Staff explained the village did not receive the TAP (Transportation Alternatives Program) grant it had applied for, meaning pedestrian crossing improvements at County Trunk X and Sternberg Avenue — identified in the West Elementary School Safe Routes to School plan — would now be fully at village expense, estimated at $150,000-$200,000 construction cost with a design fee around $45,000. The improvements include a refuge island and pedestrian-activated warning lights. The committee voted to recommend awarding the design contract, contingent on staff reviewing and aligning the consultant's liability limitation language with the village's standard contract template before execution.

discussions.item: Business 51 Storm Pond Construction Intergovernmental Agreement
discussions.body: Staff presented a construction-phase intergovernmental agreement for the Highway 29/Business 51 storm water pond shared with the Village of Rothschild and City of Schofield. Staff noted updated hydraulic modeling now shows the pond will remove 225 pounds of phosphorus annually — nearly double the originally estimated 122 pounds — which will delay the need for additional phosphorus removal projects. The village's cost share percentage increases slightly as a result, but staff framed this as favorable overall. The committee voted to recommend the village board approve the agreement.

discussions.item: Ross Avenue/Town of Weston Intergovernmental Agreement
discussions.body: Staff presented a draft intergovernmental agreement with the Town of Weston for reconstruction of Ross Avenue from Riverbend Road to Paula's Avenue, programmed for 2028 construction with a surface transportation grant covering approximately 75% of costs (over $2.2 million). The cost split is approximately 51% village and 49% town based on right-of-way analysis. The agreement includes annexation provisions so that if town land annexes to the village post-construction, the village would reimburse the town for its proportionate remaining debt payments. A committee member raised a question about whether driveways should be explicitly included in the annexation reimbursement language, and staff agreed to refine that language. The committee voted to recommend approval with possible minor clarifications on pre- and post-annexation cost provisions.

publicComment: No public comment was offered. A representative from Inpipe Technology (Sean Dudy) was present to deliver the I&I study presentation as a scheduled agenda item, not as a public commenter.

title: Rules Review Committee Meeting
committee: City of Wausau Rules Review Committee
overview: The Wausau Rules Review Committee held an organizational 'table-setting' session on November 9th to identify potential revisions to the City of Wausau's standing rules (Chapter 2.16 of municipal code). No formal votes or rule changes were made; the committee identified several areas for future revision including public comment procedures, standing committee appointments, absence notification, subcommittee chair elections, and the reporting chain from this committee to council. The committee agreed to reconvene in mid-January 2027 after members submit redlined proposed changes to the city attorney.

discussions.item: Reporting chain: committee of the whole vs. direct to council
discussions.body: Committee members, including Alder Tierney and Terry Kilian, questioned why recommendations must go to the committee of the whole before the full council, calling it redundant since the committee of the whole is essentially the same body. City Attorney Vinnie confirmed the reporting structure was set by the resolution creating this subcommittee. Mayor Doug Diny suggested the committee of the whole step allows all alders to weigh in on rule changes before council action. No formal change was made; it was noted the resolution could be amended via suspension of the rules at a future council meeting.

discussions.item: Rule 16 - public comment engagement policy
discussions.body: The chair raised whether the existing practice of not engaging with public commenters should be codified in the rules, prompted by recent media coverage. Alder Hanei argued the current practice was proper and warned against a 'knee-jerk reaction to a mischaracterization by a media outlet.' Terry Kilian said a brief response to a direct question from a commenter could be respectful and appropriate. Alder Tierney raised concerns about managing time and consistency in contentious situations. Mayor Diny noted responses have historically been limited to procedural direction from the chair, and that the practice only became controversial after media reported on it. No rule change was finalized; members were asked to submit proposed language.

discussions.item: Standing committee appointments - proposed rule addition
discussions.body: Alderperson Lou Larson raised during public comment that he and Alder Rasmussen were removed from long-held committee assignments, which he attributed to retribution. The chair noted two alders had requested a rule providing continuity for experienced alders in committee appointments. Alder Hanei and Terry Kilian both stated they were not in favor of changing the rule giving the mayor appointment authority, with Hanei noting it could undermine the mayor's prerogative and citing Marshfield's annual reappointment model as a possible alternative. No change was recommended.

discussions.item: Rule 13 - subcommittee chairs and executive committee chairperson
discussions.body: Alder Tierney argued subcommittees such as bike and pedestrian should elect their own chair and vice chair, consistent with how standing committees operate. Terry Kilian additionally questioned why the executive committee — a standing committee — is required by Rule 13H to be chaired by the council president rather than electing its own chair. The city attorney noted some boards and commissions are governed by statute and cannot be changed, but council standing committees and subcommittees are within the rules' scope. No formal change was made; proposed language would be drafted for the next meeting.

discussions.item: Suspension of rules and consent agenda efficiency
discussions.body: Alder Tierney expressed strong opposition to routine suspension of the rules, noting a previous rules committee under Gary Gelman had addressed the same recurring problem. Alder Hanei raised concerns about consent agendas containing items from committees some alders did not serve on, and suggested items that failed in committee should never appear on the consent agenda. Mayor Diny noted the old agenda software listed committee vote tallies alongside resolutions and suggested that practice be restored. The city attorney cited Rule 14 as already allowing committee chairs to give brief reports to council on their items. No rule changes were made; members encouraged to submit redlined proposals.

discussions.item: Number and structure of standing committees
discussions.body: Alder Hanei raised the question of whether the city has too many committees, noting items sometimes travel through multiple committees before reaching council. He suggested exploring whether fewer committees with more members could mean more efficient city business and broader aldermanic awareness of issues before council votes. The chair acknowledged this was raised by the mayor at the organizational meeting and said the door remains open for the committee to consider recommending structural changes. No action taken.

publicComment: One speaker offered public comment: Lou Larson, 904 South 21st Place, Wausau, identified himself as the alderperson for District 10. He raised two concerns: first, that placing public comment before the meeting sets a negative tone and risks turning council meetings into 'all-night extravaganzas' when contentious topics draw large crowds; second, that experienced alders including himself and Alder Rasmussen were removed from long-held committee assignments this term, which he characterized as retribution for disagreements with the mayor.

overview: The Marathon County Infrastructure Committee met on November 5th, 2026 and took several significant actions, most notably approving an ordinance to allow ATV/UTV access on State Highway 34 and separately voting to request the state DOT approve flashing warning signs for that segment. The committee also received updates on the 2027 budget, the routine state highway maintenance agreement, the Wausau MPO long-range transportation plan, and IT department projects, though no votes were taken on those informational items.

discussions.body: The minutes were approved without discussion. A motion was made by Watson and seconded by Coyle. The motion carried on a voice vote.

discussions.item: 2027 Annual Budget Overview
discussions.body: County Administrator Leonard and HR/Finance/Property Committee Chair Robinson presented a brief overview, noting the deadline for proposed budget amendments was 8:00 a.m. the following morning for Finance Committee review before county board adoption. Robinson highlighted that one driver of budget growth is funding for the highway facility. No amendments were proposed and no votes were taken.

discussions.item: ATV/UTV Access on State Highway 34
discussions.body: Supervisor Gal raised safety concerns about ATV/UTV traffic mixing with high-volume truck traffic on State Highway 34, citing approximately 6,000 vehicles per day compared to the county's 1,500-vehicle threshold for county trunk highways, and noting that ATVs traveling at 35 mph would share the road with trucks doing 60 mph. Jeff Gates, a member of the public, stated that hundreds of riders would use the route and that the current detour adds roughly 25 minutes of travel time. DOT representative Mike Crutchmer confirmed the DOT reviewed the draft ordinance but noted he deferred to access engineer Rich Hendrick on specifics. Vice Chair Gal moved to approve the ordinance with a condition requiring flashing warning lights; Supervisor Dickinson argued the signage question was separate and moved to divide the question into two parts. After procedural discussion involving corporation counsel, the motion was split: the original ordinance was approved unanimously on a voice vote, and a separate motion requesting the state DOT approve flashing warning signage for the ATV route on State Highway 34 passed 5-2.

discussions.item: Safe Routes to School Program and Cronin Area Request
discussions.body: Commissioner Lang explained that Marathon County's historical practice is to co-sign Safe Routes to School applications rather than serve as the primary sponsor, as the primary benefit is local. He noted the next application window is fall 2027, and that North Central Regional Planning assists communities with applications. No action was taken.

discussions.item: Routine Maintenance Agreement Update
discussions.body: Commissioner Lang and DOT Operations Manager Mike Crutchmer reviewed the annual routine maintenance agreement under which Marathon County maintains state roads. Discussion focused on cost reimbursement concerns, particularly the dramatic increase in plow blade costs — from roughly $300 to $750 for a 3-foot blade — and the inadequacy of the 5-year rolling average reimbursement rate to keep pace. Supervisors Gal and Sybert asked for data on the county's overall financial partnership with the state. No vote was taken; staff was directed to gather reimbursement and cost-sharing figures.

discussions.item: MPO Long Range Transportation Plan Update
discussions.body: Staff member Lori presented the update, noting four roadway segments identified as Level of Service D: State Highway 153/Main Street between 4th and Old Highway 51, Bridge Street over the Wisconsin River, West Thomas Street between South 3rd and Cleveland Avenue, and Grand Avenue between Townline Road and Thomas Street. The draft plan will be released for public review later in November through December. No vote was taken.

discussions.item: CCIT Projects Update
discussions.body: CCIT Director Greg Klein highlighted open enrollment IT support for the city and county, an upgrade to NetMotion VPN software across 128 squad cars to meet new criminal justice encryption requirements, and ongoing transition of network support for the UWSP campus on River Drive ahead of a January 1st handoff. A question arose about the status of the former Marathon County Credit Union building on Thomas Street, with the administrator confirming the occupant has not yet vacated. No vote was taken.

overview: The Marathon County Joint Extension, Education, Economic Development and Human Resources, Finance, and Property Committees met to consider a one-year operating lease for the former UWSP campus theater building with the Marathon Center for Arts and Culture (MCAC), and to review two new proposals for the River Drive properties. The committees approved the MCAC lease with a modification requiring the tenant to cover approximately $7,428 in annual building insurance costs, then voted to enter closed session to discuss negotiation strategy on the River Drive RFP responses.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Two speakers offered public comment. Jim Davo, Village Administrator of Kronenwetter, thanked county staff in the clerk's office, highway shop, and sheriff's department for their professionalism and cooperative work with the village. Gail Marshall, speaking by phone, urged the committees to reject the current RFP proposals for the River Drive properties, arguing the process had failed to produce meaningful results and recommending the county instead hire a commercial real estate broker — estimating a 3% commission would still yield 97% of sale proceeds to taxpayers. She also asked what the county currently insures the River Drive properties for.

discussions.body: Minutes were approved by both committees in separate motions. For the Extension, Education, and Economic Development (Triple-ED) committee, Supervisor Hagen moved and the motion was seconded; it passed. discussions.item: UWSP Campus Redevelopment Update and MCAC One-Year Lease
discussions.body: Administrator Chris Holman reported that a city feasibility study agreement is in place, building systems are being inventoried and winterized, and staff are working with the UW exit committee. The proposed one-year operating lease with the Marathon Center for Arts and Culture (MCAC) was presented to bridge the gap while MCAC finalizes its 501c3 property tax exemption with the state. Tim Parker, CEO of the Community Foundation of North Central Wisconsin and MCAC fiscal agent, told committees that 95% of office spaces are leased and theater bookings are at 60% through June, with January and February already full. Kurt Gibbs raised the issue of insurance costs, noting the building is insured for approximately $13 million and the annual premium is roughly $7,428; he argued that cost should be borne by the tenant. Vice Chair Pool moved to approve the lease with a modification directing staff to negotiate inclusion of the $7,428 insurance cost spread over monthly payments; the motion was seconded and passed.

discussions.item: River Drive RFP Proposals – Raise and Roast Cafe (Oswald)
discussions.body: Justin and Elena Oswald presented their proposal to purchase 210 River Drive for $1 to develop 'Raise and Roast Cafe,' envisioning an affordable community cafe on the ground floor and a fundraising event venue on the second floor, with free recreational activities and partnerships with downtown institutions. Holman noted the proposal has strong alignment with criteria for activating unused property, community benefit, and local ownership, with moderate alignment on job creation and tax base reactivation. No formal vote or counter-offer was made in open session.

discussions.item: River Drive RFP Proposals – VFW Post 388 Veterans and Community Campus
discussions.body: Tamara Sillers, VFW Post 388 events coordinator, presented the VFW's proposal to acquire all three River Drive buildings (210, 212, and 326) to create a veterans and community campus, with 210 as an event venue, 212 as a community lounge with mental health counseling space and bingo, and 326 as garage and storage. She noted the VFW vacated River Drive around 2017 and the move was a mistake for community connectivity. Supervisors questioned how the new model differs from the bar-and-restaurant model that led to the prior departure, the organization's current revenue sources, and its nonprofit status (501c19). Holman disclosed the appraised market value of the River Drive parcel at $2,268,000 (land $87,000, improvements $1,261,000 as of November 2025) and insurance values: 210 at $2,635,700, 212 at $3,734,400, and 326 at $1,271,100. The presiding chair expressed disappointment at dollar-sale proposals given significant county investment, stating an obligation to taxpayers to maximize return.

overview: The Kronenwetter Plan Commission held its November 4, 2026 meeting primarily to deliberate and act on a conditional use permit for Eau Claire River LLC to operate an aggregate mine and pond expansion at 1320 Kowalski Road. After extensive discussion of operating conditions, noise, flood storage, and future development potential, the commission unanimously approved the CUP 7-0 with conditions. The decision is significant to residents as it sets the stage for potential industrial development of a long-stalled TIF district property by creating flood storage capacity that could unlock adjacent parcels.

discussions.item: Conditional Use Permit - Eau Claire River LLC, 1320 Kowalski Road
discussions.body: The commission deliberated extensively on the CUP for an approximately 35.58-acre aggregate mining and pond expansion operation. Community Development Director Nathan Sandwick (referred to as 'Nathan' throughout) guided the commission through findings of fact and proposed conditions. Applicant representatives Tom and Gary provided extensive background on the site's history, flood storage engineering, prior interchange planning discussions, the settlement agreement with the Diocese that led to dropping a lawsuit, and confirmed no blasting or asphalt batching plant would occur. After working through roughly 14 proposed condition bullet points, the commission agreed to include conditions on: permitted hours of operation (6 a.m.–7 p.m. Monday–Friday, 6 a.m.–noon Saturday, year-round); a five-year renewal review period; perimeter staking of the excavation area; requiring trucks to be covered to suppress dust and debris; implementation of a reclamation plan; compliance with Village erosion and stormwater control standards; a geotechnical analysis by a qualified engineer to confirm excavation will not compromise adjacent roadways; and compliance with all applicable laws. Conditions on road repair monitoring, specific noise monitoring by either party, and redundant buffer yard language already covered by code were not included.

overview: The Wausau Economic Development Committee met on November 4th and took action on three substantive items: authorizing staff to prepare a TID 8 project plan amendment for infrastructure projects, approving the $1 purchase of a tax-delinquent property at 108 Myron Street for future affordable housing, and debating a deed restriction and resolution for city-owned property at 1300 Cleveland Avenue. The Cleveland Avenue item resulted in a procedural deadlock, with a 2-2 tie on the amended resolution, sending the matter to the full city council on November 24th with section 4 removed from the deed restriction.

discussions.item: TID 8 Project Plan Amendment
discussions.body: Director Fifick explained the amendment would authorize staff to engage a consultant to draft a project plan amendment for Tax Increment District 8, adding infrastructure project costs including lead service line replacement, asphalt overlay, 17th Avenue reconstruction, water and sewer upgrades, and traffic signal replacement. Alder Killian expressed she was not prepared to vote without knowing whether lead line replacement funding covered private or entire replacement, but the motion carried 3-1. Staff noted the item had already been approved 5-0 at the Finance Committee and was placed on the November city council agenda.

discussions.item: Purchase of County-Owned Property at 108 Myron Street
discussions.body: Staff member Tammy presented details on the tax-delinquent property, which has been vacant for years due to a broken pipe causing black mold, rendering it too dangerous to enter. The county approved the city's $1 offer unanimously on October 20th, with full county board consideration set for November 10th. Funding for purchase and demolition would come from Community Development Block Grant funds, not tax levy, with DPW performing the demolition. The end goal is disposition for affordable housing for income-qualifying households. Alder Killian expressed safety concerns about demolition given the black mold but said she would support the motion. Alder Lukans noted for viewers that CDBG/HUD funds, not taxpayer levy money, would be used. The motion carried unanimously by voice vote.

discussions.item: Deed Restriction and Resolution for 1300 Cleveland Avenue
discussions.body: Director Fifick and the committee debated a draft deed restriction prohibiting industrial uses on the city-owned property at 1300 Cleveland Avenue, while preserving existing non-conforming uses including Marathon County/Wausau Parks log and wood chip storage and DPW training approved by a 2024 resolution. Alder Tierney's written comments, read into the record by Director Fifick, argued that non-conforming uses should end and the property cleaned up as promised to neighbors. Parks representative Jamie testified that relocating log storage requires council direction on an alternative site of approximately one acre, noting the ongoing Emerald Ash Borer program creates continuous need. Mayor Diny reported that fire training had already been relocated, and miscellaneous DPW equipment and a trailer had been cleaned up. Alder Killian moved an amendment to remove section 4A from the deed restriction, discontinue DPW training by February 1st, and give Parks 6 months to relocate; that amendment failed 2-2. Chair Heniki then moved a narrower amendment to remove only section 4 from the deed restriction, which passed 3-1. The main motion on the resolution as amended then failed 2-2, sending the matter to the November 24th city council meeting with section 4 removed from the deed restriction and a redrafted resolution to be prepared by staff.

overview: The Marathon County Environmental Resources Committee held its November 3, 2026 meeting, conducting four rezoning public hearings and several town zoning reviews. The most significant action was the committee's decision to postpone a contested farmland preservation-to-low-density-residential rezoning request (MK7 Enterprises LLC in the Town of Marathon) to allow the town additional time to respond, following substantial opposition from neighbors, an attorney representing adjacent landowners, and a local farmer who owns surrounding acreage. Three other rezoning petitions were approved without significant opposition.

discussions.item: 5A1: Weissaki Rezoning - General Agriculture to Rural Estate, Town of Green Valley
discussions.body: Staff presenter Garrett Pogle reported that both the Town of Green Valley and county staff recommended approval. Adjacent property owner William Kaiser raised concerns about an old dump on the property, including potential groundwater contamination and who would bear responsibility. Pogle explained that any new property owner inherits responsibility for existing violations, but that the dump predates the 10-year enforcement window, limiting the county's authority to act. The committee approved the rezoning to forward to the county board.

discussions.item: 5A2: Schultz Rezoning - Rural Residential to Rural Estate, Town of McMillan
discussions.body: Pogle reported that both the Town of McMillan and county staff recommended approval of the rezoning. No public comment was offered. The committee approved the motion without notable debate, with Supervisor Drebeck moving and Supervisor Shamborn seconding.

discussions.item: 5A3: MK7 Enterprises LLC Rezoning - Farmland Preservation to Low Density Residential, Town of Marathon
discussions.body: This was the most contested item of the meeting. Attorney Anders Helquist of Weld Riley Law Firm argued on behalf of adjacent property owners that the application failed all four statutory requirements to rezone out of farmland preservation, noting that the applicant's own application admitted two of the four standards were not met, that future land use maps show the parcel as agricultural/woodland, and that there were conflicts with surrounding agricultural uses. Local farmer Tyler Sehafer, who owns surrounding acreage, warned of road infrastructure inadequacy, grain bin noise conflicts, and noted that 100% of approximately 30 residents at a prior town meeting opposed the project. Land surveyor Dan Higinbotham, associated with the project, testified that wetland delineation was underway and soil evaluations were scheduled for the following Tuesday. Additional opposition came from Town of Marathon residents Randall Walcott and Karen Milbeck, who cited misleading communications about the project's intent and concerns about road damage from log trucks. Committee members debated extensively, with Chair Ritter noting a potential inconsistency with how the committee had handled a prior Town of Green Valley case based on future land use maps. Corporation Counsel advised that if a denial motion was made, it needed substantive reasons on the record. A motion to approve by Supervisor Sefelt failed for lack of a second. A denial motion by Supervisor Bro was ruled out of order by the chair after Corporation Counsel indicated it relied on factors not properly before the board (septic suitability). The committee ultimately voted to postpone the matter to no later than the January ERC meeting to give the Town of Marathon an opportunity to respond.

discussions.item: 5A4: Spencer Joint Revocable Trust Rezoning - Farmland Preservation to General Agriculture, Town of McMillan
discussions.body: Staff reported that both the Town of McMillan and county staff recommended approval. No public comment was offered. Supervisor Shamborn moved to approve based on findings of fact, conclusions of law, and the town's recommendation; the motion carried without notable debate.

discussions.item: 5B1 & 5B2: Town Zoning Changes - Town of Castle and Town of Weston
discussions.body: Both town-initiated zoning changes were presented by staff as having met all application requirements. Town of Castle sought a partial rezone from farmland to M1 Light Industrial; Town of Weston sought a rezone of Bowman Dairy Farm LLC property from Rural Residential 5-acre to Rural Residential 2-acre. Both were approved by the committee without public comment or significant debate.

title: Board (Budget Hearing)
overview: The Marathon County Board of Supervisors held its annual budget hearing on November 2, 2026 for the proposed 2027 budget. HR Finance Committee Chair Robinson and County Administrator Leonard presented a status quo budget that drops the property tax rate by one cent to $3.48, funds a new highway facility without new debt, and maintains current service levels. Three members of the public testified, two raising concerns about the county's Flock license plate reader camera system and one questioning the highway facility funding strategy.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Overview
discussions.body: HR Finance Committee Chair Robinson outlined the year-long budget development process including a 'bucket challenge' prioritization exercise by board members, review of fees, and direction to avoid new debt. Administrator Leonard presented key budget metrics: the property tax rate drops one cent to $3.48, equalized value grew 6.25%, net new construction was 1.545%, and the county ranks 13th lowest in per capita spending statewide. Leonard emphasized the highway facility funding plan — moving the $3.5 million North Central Healthcare payment onto the debt levy to avoid new borrowing for the nearly $55 million project — as the cornerstone of the budget.

discussions.item: Social Services Department Staffing Increases
discussions.body: Supervisor Sundowski questioned a proposed increase of 12 positions and roughly $4 million in the Social Services budget. Administrator Leonard and Social Services Director Christa explained that the Children's Long-Term Support (CLTS) social worker positions are fully federally funded through Medicaid billing and driven by state wait-list requirements, while the economic support specialist positions are funded through a state contract related to federal quality assurance requirements tied to the 'big beautiful bill.' Leonard clarified that positions are added incrementally as caseloads require, and that if funding streams disappear, the positions are eliminated without board action.

discussions.item: Highway Facility Funding Strategy
discussions.body: Supervisor Cavelli and Supervisor Nisth questioned the phased implementation of the highway facility debt levy strategy, citing concerns raised by former supervisor David Baker in public testimony. Baker had argued that placing the full $3.5 million NCHC payment on the debt levy in year one contradicted the phased approach described in Resolution 4926, and asked whether proceeds from property sales or reserves could reduce the $25 million funding gap. Administrator Leonard defended the approach, explaining that delay increases risk of having to borrow for other capital projects in 2029-2031, and that proceeds from the sale of West Street shop, 28th Avenue parcels, and the Thomas Street property (400 East Thomas) could shorten the inter-fund loan period but are best evaluated after the annual audit.

discussions.item: Flock License Plate Reader System — Budget Implications
discussions.body: Following public testimony from Courtney Olsen and Felix Gallow calling for defunding the Flock camera system, Supervisor Morash asked what budget options exist. Administrator Leonard explained that grant funds for the original five cameras are fully expended and $6,300 is in the sheriff's budget to continue that contract through the remainder of 2027; a second grant covering three cameras does not expire until March 2029 with no budget funds required. Sheriff Bip addressed the board, defending the technology as a legitimate law enforcement tool, stating that searches require a case number and are limited to specific personnel, that data is not shared with private entities, that audits occur twice monthly, and that the system is not used for immigration enforcement. Supervisor Robinson announced he had arranged a meeting between the sheriff and Gallow to work toward resolution. The board agreed to refer detailed discussion to the November 10 Public Safety Committee meeting.

discussions.item: User Fees and Equity Concerns
discussions.body: Supervisor Leur raised concerns that increased user fees disproportionately burden lower-income residents and asked whether the county tracks the impact of fee increases on service utilization. Administrator Leonard acknowledged the concern, noted that the marriage license fee was deliberately not increased at the county clerk's recommendation, and emphasized that fee-setting is ultimately a board policy decision. He also noted two additional fee changes — a professional services fee in the medical examiner's office and minor solid waste adjustments — would be brought to the board before final budget adoption.

publicComment: Three speakers testified at the formal public hearing. Courtney Olsen, executive director of a domestic violence agency, asked the board to amend the 2027 budget to prohibit county funds from being used for Flock or any license plate reader contract without a public hearing and board vote, and to request a corporate counsel opinion on board authority and county liability. Felix Gallow, also a Wausau resident, asked the board to prohibit budget funds from going to Flock without additional board study, and requested the sheriff commit to mandatory audits with oversight, quarterly public reports, and limiting data sharing to adjacent jurisdictions, state patrol, and DCI. David Baker of Kronenwetter supported the new highway facility and the no-new-debt strategy but questioned why the full $3.5 million payment was placed on the debt levy in year one rather than phased in, and asked the board to consider using property sale proceeds and reserves to reduce the $25 million funding gap.

title: Common Council Meeting
overview: The Wausau Common Council held its October 27, 2026 meeting, addressing a wide range of items including a detailed stormwater utility feasibility study presentation, routine resolutions, and a significant debate over the city's Flock license plate reader camera system. The council voted 8-2 to suspend rules and ultimately passed a resolution directing the appropriate city department to cease use of Flock data and physically cover all Flock cameras within two business weeks, reflecting sustained public and council pressure over privacy and data misuse concerns.
